overview.summary: New Zealand manufacturing covers food and beverage, wood products, machinery, metal fabrication, chemicals, plastics, electronics and other specialised production. Many firms compete through niche design, quality, responsiveness and export relationships rather than global scale. Earnings depend on throughput, yield, labour productivity, input and energy costs, pricing, product quality, plant reliability and the working capital tied up from raw material through finished goods and receivables.
business_models: Make-to-stock production serving distributors, retailers or export markets
Make-to-order or engineer-to-order production for defined customers and projects
Contract manufacturing earning conversion margin using customer specifications or materials
Branded food, beverage or consumer-product manufacturing
Component, fabrication and industrial-service manufacturing with after-sales or maintenance income
industry_structure: The sector is diverse and often composed of SMEs serving specialist domestic or export niches.
Scale, automation and procurement can improve unit cost, but flexible short runs and technical capability can support niche operators.
Customer qualification, product certification and tooling can create stickiness, while concentration and offshore competition remain risks.
demand_drivers: Domestic construction, agriculture, consumer demand and industrial investment
Export demand, exchange rates, trade access and overseas distributor performance
Customer product cycles, specifications, replacement and maintenance
Innovation, sustainability requirements and local supply-chain resilience
margin_and_cost_drivers: Capacity utilisation, batch size, labour efficiency, machine uptime and yield
Raw materials, freight, energy, packaging, waste and foreign exchange
Pricing lag, product mix, quality failures and warranty or recall cost
Maintenance, tooling, certification and sustainable replacement capex
cyclicality_and_seasonality: Exposure varies by end market: construction materials and capital equipment may be cyclical, while food can be more defensive.
Agricultural inputs, export shipping and customer ordering may create seasonal production and inventory peaks.
Engineer-to-order operations can show lumpy revenue and work-in-progress movements.
overview.working_capital_profile: Manufacturers fund raw materials, work in progress and finished goods before collection. Lead times, minimum order quantities, safety stock, batch economics, customer terms and import content can make growth cash-consuming. Inventory records must distinguish usable, slow, obsolete, customer-specific and consigned stock, while WIP valuation depends on accurate routing, labour and overhead allocation.
overview.asset_intensity: Plant, tooling, property improvements and maintenance are often material. Book depreciation may not equal economic replacement. Specialised equipment can have low alternative-use or forced-sale value despite high replacement cost. Capacity, condition, downtime, compliance and the capital required to sustain output are central to valuation and lending.
regulatory_and_compliance: Health and Safety at Work duties for machinery, mobile plant, dust, fumes, noise and hazardous substances
Food, product, electrical, building, environmental or export certification relevant to output
Resource consents, waste, emissions and energy requirements
Product quality, traceability, recall, warranty and importer or supplier duties

subsectors.name: Food and beverage manufacturing
subsectors.business_model: Ingredients are processed and packaged for retail, food service or export under owned or customer brands.
subsectors.working_capital: Shelf life, seasonal inputs and finished stock require disciplined planning and traceability.
subsectors.asset_intensity: Processing, packaging, cold storage and compliance assets can be significant.

subsectors.name: Metal, machinery and engineering manufacturing
subsectors.business_model: Components, equipment or fabricated assemblies are produced to standard or customer design.
subsectors.working_capital: Customer-specific WIP and long-lead materials can be difficult to redeploy if an order changes.
subsectors.asset_intensity: Machine tools, cranes, welding and testing equipment require maintenance and renewal.

subsectors.name: Wood and building-product manufacturing
subsectors.business_model: Timber, panels, joinery or other building inputs are processed for construction and distribution.
subsectors.working_capital: Raw and finished stock can be bulky, seasonal and exposed to construction cycles.
subsectors.asset_intensity: Saws, presses, dust extraction and production property are material.

subsectors.name: Contract and advanced manufacturing
subsectors.business_model: Technical production is performed for customers using specialised process capability, quality systems and sometimes customer-owned designs.
subsectors.working_capital: Components may be imported with long lead times; customer programme changes can strand stock.
subsectors.asset_intensity: Automation, clean or controlled environments, testing and technical systems can be material.

primary_risks.mechanism: Materials, energy, freight, wages or foreign exchange may rise before prices reset.
Volume loss or breakdowns reduce absorption, while deferred maintenance can overstate cash generation.
Long lead items and customer-specific stock may not be recoverable after cancellation or demand change.
Injury, recall, certification loss or environmental breach can stop production and create claims.

cash_conversion_and_working_capital: Reconcile physical stock to perpetual records and test aging, ownership and net realisable value.
Review WIP by customer order, stage, margin, cancellation rights and recoverability.
Model material lead times, minimum orders and the working-capital effect of growth.
Measure free cash after normal maintenance, tooling and replacement capex.
collateral_considerations: Plant needs serial, ownership, prior-security, condition and current orderly and forced-sale values.
Specialised equipment may have low realisable value despite high replacement cost.
Inventory eligibility should exclude obsolete, customer-owned, consigned and highly specific stock.
IP, certifications and customer tooling may be operationally critical but difficult collateral.
downside_stresses: Loss of a major programme with incomplete variable-cost removal
Input-cost increase with delayed price recovery
Inventory write-down and slower receivable collection
monitoring_kpis: Sales and gross margin by product and customer
Inventory and WIP days and aging
On-time delivery, rejects, warranty and incidents
covenant_considerations: Borrowing-base controls and reporting triggers for customer loss, plant outage or recall
diligence_questions: Which products and customers generate contribution after scrap, rework, freight and support?
How much inventory or WIP is customer-specific, aged, imported or subject to ownership restrictions?
What plant replacement, maintenance and compliance spend is required over the debt term?
What happens to margin under lower utilisation and delayed pricing?
Are quality, safety, environmental and product certifications current and transferable?

value_drivers: Defensible technical capability, IP, qualification and customer switching costs
Reliable, compliant plant with funded replacement
Management and engineering depth beyond the owner
multiple_influences: Recurring qualified programmes and proprietary products can be more predictable than project or commodity production.
High replacement cost does not equal market value, and deferred capex lowers cash-flow quality.
Customer concentration, customer-owned IP and single-site risk reduce transferability.
normalisation_focus: Normal scrap, warranty and quality cost
Related-party property rent and R&D classification
peer_selection: Match product and end market, make-to-stock versus order, branded versus contract, export mix and asset intensity.
Compare customer concentration, margin, utilisation, plant age, growth and certification.
Avoid combining food, commodity building products and advanced technical manufacturing without clear adjustments.
preferred_metrics: EV/revenue only where gross margin and product economics closely align
DCF or free cash flow after working capital and capex
discount_and_premium_factors: Premium indicators include proprietary capability, qualified recurring programmes, strong yields and diversified demand.
Discount indicators include capex catch-up, customer-specific stock, plant bottlenecks, recall risk and owner-held know-how.
diligence_questions: What portion of earnings is sustainable at normal utilisation and input prices?
What capital and working capital are needed for the forecast?
Who owns product IP, tooling and customer qualifications?
Can technical, quality and sales capability transfer without the owner?

market_research_sections.credit_paper:
Manufacturing in New Zealand is diverse, ranging from food and building products to metal, machinery and advanced technical production. MBIE's advanced-manufacturing material describes opportunities around capability and transformation, while WorkSafe identifies machinery, vehicles, dust, fumes and hazardous substances as important sector risks. These sources frame the operating environment; credit quality still depends on the subject's customers, products, utilisation, plant, inventory and controls.

A lender should bridge revenue to gross margin and cash by product and customer. Input prices, foreign exchange, labour, energy, yield, scrap, downtime and delayed repricing can materially change EBITDA. Growth commonly consumes cash through raw materials, work in progress, finished goods and receivables. Inventory and WIP require aging, ownership and recoverability tests, especially where components are imported or customer-specific. Debt service must be measured after sustainable maintenance, tooling and replacement capex.

Plant can support security, but specialisation, condition, removal cost, prior liens and secondary-market depth drive recovery rather than replacement or book value. Quality, product recall, certification, environmental and worker-safety failures can interrupt production. The credit paper should stress lower utilisation, price-recovery lag, plant outage and stock write-down, then link monitoring and conditions to the borrower's actual sub-sector and control environment.
market_research_sections.valuation_report:
Manufacturing value reflects sustainable cash generated from products, customers, process capability and plant—not the replacement cost of machinery alone. New Zealand firms often compete in specialist niches through design, responsiveness, quality or qualification. Valuation should therefore identify whether the subject is branded, contract, make-to-stock, engineer-to-order or advanced manufacturing, and match peers by end market, gross margin, customer concentration, export exposure and asset intensity.

Maintainable earnings need to reflect normal utilisation, input prices, yield, scrap, warranty, owner engineering and sales remuneration and sustainable plant and tooling expenditure. Working-capital requirements can be substantial, particularly with long-lead imports, WIP and safety stock. Deferred maintenance may temporarily lift free cash and EBITDA multiples but weakens future cash flow. Customer-owned designs, tooling or approvals must not be treated as owned intangible value.

Transferable value is stronger where technical capability is documented across a team, customer programmes are diversified and recurring, pricing and purchasing controls are effective, plant is reliable and compliant, and IP and certifications transfer. Concentrated programmes, customer-specific obsolete stock, single-site bottlenecks, capex catch-up, recall exposure and owner-held know-how increase risk. Current comparable and transaction evidence remains necessary for any market multiple.

limitations: Manufacturing economics vary materially by product, process, end market and asset intensity.
Plant condition, capacity, stock, WIP, IP, customer qualification and compliance require company-specific evidence.
The MBIE Industry Transformation Plan is historical sector context; the programme has ended and must not be described as current policy.
No current multiple, beta, plant appraisal or inventory recovery value is supplied.
